title: Ali's letter to Malik al-Ashtar
hookLine: people are either your brother in faith or your equal in creation
tomorrow: can an email be fair? a ruler's letters say yes.

lines: WHAT IS A STRANGER TO YOU?
cards: The cashier, the driver, the voice on the support line: strangers you may never see again, who still hear your tone on your worst day. Nothing ties you to them: no family, no team, maybe no shared faith.
So what is a stranger to you? Ali, the Prophet's cousin, answered in a letter to the man he sent to govern Egypt, Malik al-Ashtar.

teach.b: The letter is kept in Nahj al-Balagha, a collection of Ali's sermons and letters. Fill your heart with mercy for the people, he tells Malik, with love for them and kindness toward them. Don't be a predator over them.

For people are of two kinds: either your brother in faith, or your equal in creation. They will slip and make mistakes, so forgive them as you'd want God to forgive you. Faith is one bond, and a real one.
It isn't the only one. Everyone under Malik's rule, sharing his faith or not, is owed the same mercy, because the same God made them. Here's a neighbor who asks it as a question.
In the Hebrew Bible, read by Jews and Christians, the prophet Malachi says: “Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us?” Shared ground: both root the bond between people in one Creator.
One honest difference: readers of Malachi differ on whether the father there is God or an ancestor, and the prophet is calling his own people to keep faith with each other.
Muslims don't call God father, and Ali writes an order to a governor about how power treats everyone. Two voices, one question, neither needing to become the other.

how: Ali's letter to Malik al-Ashtar is studied by Shia and Sunni readers as a guide to just government; its line on the two kinds of people is often quoted when Muslims speak of human dignity.

games.q: what does “ali's letter to malik al-ashtar” mean?
o: Ali's orders to his governor: mercy for all people
a treaty Ali signed with a neighboring ruler
a poem Ali wrote in praise of the city of Kufa

games.q: the letter and its neighbor — tap the pairs.
p: have we not all one father?

s: Ali's letter tells Malik to be kind mainly to fellow Muslims
he names two kinds, brother in faith or equal in creation, and asks mercy for both.
the letter asks Malik to forgive people's slips as he'd want God to forgive him
they will slip and err, so pardon them.
Malachi's question and Ali's line say exactly the same thing
both name one Creator; Malachi calls his own people back, Ali instructs a governor.

games.q: you're the new captain of a team where some players share your faith and some don't. who gets your patience?
o: all of them, the same: brother in faith or equal in creation.
the ones who share your faith first, then the others.
nobody in particular; faith shouldn't come up at all.
games.why: Ali names two bonds and gives both the same mercy. faith is real, but it isn't where kindness stops.

practice: Close your eyes and bring back one stranger from this week: a cashier, a driver, a voice on the phone. Hold their face as clearly as you can. Then, silently, give them the name from the letter: equal in creation.

wordCard.voice: Ali's letter to Malik al-Ashtar: Ali's instructions to his governor, where people are your brother in faith or your equal in creation.

orig.note: Arabic: nazirun laka fi al-khalq, your equal in creation, from Ali's letter.

carryVoice: The line for today: equal in creation, every stranger included. Back tomorrow for the week's look back.
